title: Console guided quant tuning session — INT8 vs FP8 latency/quality
summary: Redwood SE demo of the Console Optimize flow for tuning quantization profiles. Walkthrough compared INT8 and FP8 under CuraWave's clinical inference workload, covered latency vs quality tradeoffs, KV cache/seqlen behavior, and pilot next steps. Customer concerns: hallucination risk post-quant, HIPAA data handling, and benchmarking reproducibility.
next_steps: Avery to share end-to-end pilot proposal and pricing by 2025-07-15
Marcus to export the benchmark script and initial traces for CuraWave to reproduce locally
Jordan to confirm sample prompt set and clinical eval metrics by 2025-07-18
action_items: Avery - send pilot SOW + pricing - due 2025-07-15
Marcus - upload benchmark script + runbook to shared drive - due 2025-07-12
Jordan - provide historic query distribution and 1000-sample prompt set - due 2025-07-18
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-10 14:00 PT | Duration: ~48m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood Product), Jordan Reyes (CuraWave - Dir ML), Priya Nair (CuraWave - Infra), Sam O'Neill (CuraWave - NLP), Becky (CuraWave - Procurement)

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call — if you can say hi and your role that'd help for notes.
[00:08] Jordan: Hey it's Jordan, leads ML infra and model infra at CuraWave.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, infra, mostly network and security.
[00:15] Sam: Sam, NLP engineer, I'll be driving the eval side.
[00:18] Becky: Becky on procurement, here for timelines and contracts.
[00:21] Avery: Great. Marcus and Lina from Redwood will do the demo, just high-level: we're focusing on Console Optimize quantization profiles — INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs — and how that maps to your clinical inference SLOs.
[00:33] Marcus: Yep. I'll share my screen, show the Optimize tab, the qprofile picker, and run a short latency/quality comparison against a sample of your prompts. Heads up transcripts might drop some product names — qprofile sometimes shows up as cue-profile in transcripts, ha.
[00:46] [01:15] Marcus (screen): Ok, console open. On the left is the model catalog, we selected an open LLM family similar to what you run — 13B-ish — we've attached two qprofiles: a default FP16 baseline, an INT8 aggressive, and a middle-ground FP8 candidate.
[01:35] Sam: Quick question — our typical seqlen is 512 with KV cache usage on multi-turn notes, will the batching behavior change with INT8?
[01:42] Marcus: Good question. For your seqlen distribution, INT8 can actually reduce memory travelling but sometimes causes longer per-token compute if kernels are mismatched— you may see micro-variance at tail latencies. FP8 tends to maintain throughput while giving better numeric headroom on generative quality.
[02:05] Jordan: We're very worried about hallucinations after quant, we've seen small but meaningful shifts in clinical fact recalling. How deterministic are these differences?
[02:13] Lina: We expect small deltas; Optimize includes a quality delta view across prompt sets. You'll see predicted P99 latency, token cost, and a "regression" score based on your supplied evals. It's not perfect but surfaces prompts that degrade the most.
[02:34] [03:10] Marcus: I'll kick off a quick AB between FP16 and INT8 using Sam's 200-sample subset you uploaded earlier. Running now — console shows the batch going to our dedicated test pool. Note: we masked PHI tokens locally — we used placeholders in the sample to avoid PHI in our environment.
[03:34] Sam: Thanks. Also curious if the KV cache evictions differ — we use streaming notes so cache behavior matters.
[03:40] Marcus: Right. INT8 profiles sometimes have narrower KV element SIMD widths so cache hits are similar but evictions pattern can be slightly different. We'll show the token-level latency breakdown.
[04:05] [05:00] Marcus (console): Results are in. FP16 baseline — mean latency 120ms/token, P95 230ms. INT8 — mean 88ms/token, P95 210ms. FP8 — mean 95ms/token, P95 205ms. Quality delta: INT8 shows a 6% drop in Rouge-like similarity on your eval set, FP8 shows 2% drop. Again this is for this sample set.
[05:27] Jordan: 6% is... not negligible. Do you have examples where INT8 fails medical recall?
[05:34] Marcus: I pulled two examples — here's one: prompt asking for a guideline citation — FP16 returns the expected line, INT8 returned a plausible but incorrect guideline number. It's a subtle numeric hallucination.
[05:45] Sam: That's the kind of failure we can't accept in prod without an extra safety layer.
[05:49] Avery: Totally understood. There are a few levers: 1) pick FP8 as a compromise; 2) use INT8 only for non-clinical pathways (e.g., search summaries) and keep FP16 for factual recall; 3) enable prompt-level regression gating in our Console so any prompt with >X degradation falls back to FP16.
[06:15] Priya: That gating sounds interesting. Does it add much latency or cost?
[06:19] Marcus: Minimal. It routes at the request level: quick eval of a small embedding or a checksum against a cached score — it's a sub-ms routing decision, the heavy path is just the model execution. There's a tiny cost for additional checks but it avoids catastrophic hallucinations.
[06:40] [08:00] Jordan: We also need auditability — if we do a pilot, we'll need proof that the quantized model didn't touch PHI in Redwood test runs.
[08:07] Lina: We run masked datasets for demo runs; for Private deployments we can operate inside your VPC or on-prem where we never see tokens. For Dedicated hosted pilots we provide detailed access logs and a redaction proof — we can provide a whitepaper on that.
[08:28] Priya: Share that whitepaper and SOC2 appendix. We need to show security to compliance.
[08:33] Becky: From procurement, timeline question: if we move forward, how long to stand up a pilot and get performance baselines?
[08:40] Avery: Typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: week 1 data prep and prompt set, week 2 baseline runs and qprofile sweep, week 3 focused QA and gating rules, week 4 wrap-up and SOW for Dedicated if you want to commit. We'll send a formal SOW.
[09:01] [10:05] Marcus: Back to the console, I'm going to show the optimize sweep UI — you can select a metric to optimize (latency, cost, or minimize quality regression). For CuraWave you might select: minimize P95 latency subject to <2% Rouge delta on clinical recall. The optimizer proposes candidate qprofiles and simulates throughput.
[10:28] Sam: How deterministic are the sims? I want to reproduce locally, maybe on our on-prem GPU fleet.
[10:33] Marcus: We export the benchmark script; it uses a dockerized harness and the same request sequence. Two caveats: kernel-level perf depends on hardware microcode and cuDNN/driver versions, and quant kernels vary across GPU arch. We'll include the exact driver/kernel matrix used in the run.
[10:54] Jordan: If the hardware differences change the ranking of INT8 vs FP8, will Redwood support re-tuning per-target-hardware?
[11:01] Lina: Yes, qprofiles are per-arch. The Console stores per-region/per-hardware profiles and the smart router can pick the best variant at runtime.
[11:15] [12:30] Marcus: I'm going to toggle a "conservative INT8" profile — it's an INT8-like memory layout but keeps certain normalization ops in FP16 to preserve numerics. Results: latency improves 40% vs FP16, and quality delta drops to 2.5% vs the aggressive INT8 6%.
[12:51] Sam: That's promising. Could that be the default for our multi-turn notes?
[12:56] Avery: Probably yes, especially since you prioritize recall. Also, you could A/B route 10% traffic to the conservative INT8 to validate in prod.
[13:10] [14:40] Jordan: On the evaluation front, we need a stricter clinical metric than Rouge; we'll provide an entity-level recall + false-positive rate set for 200 examples. Can the console ingest that?
[14:49] Marcus: Yep — Console Optimize accepts custom eval hooks. You can upload CSV with expected entities and we'll compute delta metrics and highlight prompts with regressions.
[15:05] Sam: Do you support differential privacy or noise injection during the runs? We might want to obfuscate some tokens even in logs.
[15:12] Lina: We have redaction and field-level hashing for logs. For Private deployment you get full control; for Hosted we can provide hashed traces and attestations.
[15:28] [16:50] Priya: Network question — when using Dedicated or Private, do we need egress firewall rules? Our security team worries about callback endpoints.
[16:58] Marcus: Dedicated runs in a customer VPC peered or sidecar; Private on-prem requires no egress. For hosted Dedicated there are fixed egress endpoints you allow; we'll provide a list.
[17:12] Becky: On billing — if we use mixed qprofiles, do you meter per-token with the profile multiplier?
[17:20] Avery: Billing is per-token executed with modifiers for model family and qprofile. The Console shows token cost estimates by route. We'll include an example cost sheet.
[17:32] [19:05] Marcus (demo): I'll trigger a simulated 1k request batch with mixed routing: 80% FP16, 15% conservative-INT8, 5% aggressive-INT8. Here's the cost breakdown and latencies, and the Console flagged ~12 prompts with >3% quality regression and recommended automatic fallback.
[19:25] Jordan: Can fallback be synchronous? We want end-to-end persistence — if one fails we retry with FP16.
[19:30] Marcus: Yes, fallback policies can be sync; you get a deterministic attempt with no user-visible error if configured.
[19:40] Sam: Any guidance on tokenization effects? We've noticed different tokenizers cause rounding differences in counts and occasionally impact prompt-level deltas.
[19:48] Marcus: We surface tokenizer counts and normalized token-level diffs. For your clinical notes you might canonicalize templates to reduce variance. Console has a quick preprocessor to normalize dates and IDs.
[20:05] [22:00] Jordan: Let's talk acceptance criteria: for us to accept a pilot result we need P95 latency under 350ms for our average 512 seq with <2% entity recall delta and full audit logs for runs. Can you meet that in pilot?
[22:14] Marcus: On our test runs we hit P95 ~205ms with FP8 and ~210ms with conservative-INT8 on our cluster. With your fleet there will be variations; but pilot is designed exactly to validate that.
[22:30] Lina: We'll commit to the SLO targets in the pilot SOW as milestone checks.
[22:45] Priya: If we do private deployment later, what's the uplift on ops? We need to know support SLA.
[22:52] Avery: Private deployment has a platform fee plus a support band — we'll include options in the SOW (24x7 or business hours). Private also lets you use your KMS/HSM for keys.
[23:10] [25:00] Marcus: I'm going to demonstrate the regression inspector: you can click a prompt and see side-by-side FP16/INT8 outputs with token-level attention heatmaps. This is how you triage hallucinations.
[25:22] Sam: Love that. Can we export those diffs to our issue tracker for triage?
[25:28] Marcus: Yes — one-click export to CSV or Jira.
[25:40] Jordan: Any recommended safety layers beyond fallback? We have a clinical rules engine upstream.
[25:46] Marcus: Use a hybrid: conservative INT8 for most, FP16 for high-risk calls, fallback if regression score > threshold, and post-filter with your rules engine. Also consider embedding-based rerank to boost factual retrieval.
[26:10] [28:00] Becky: Contract stuff — what's needed to get procurement moving?
[28:05] Avery: We'll share a pilot SOW, security packet (SOC2, whitepaper), and standard MSA with DPA redlines. If you can get PO or a signed SOW we can start onboarding.
[28:25] Becky: I'll need pricing line items for pilot and for a 12-month Dedicated commit.
[28:31] Avery: We'll include both in the proposal.
[28:40] [30:15] Marcus: Quick note about regression stability: some prompts flip-flop across runs due to non-determinism in GPU kernels; Optimize tracks per-prompt variance and flags flakey cases so you can exclude them from pass/fail metrics.
[30:32] Jordan: That's useful — otherwise we'd chase ghosts.
[30:40] Sam: On reproducibility, can you seed runs to be deterministic?
[30:44] Marcus: We can seed where the model supports it, but beam/non-deterministic sampling strategies still vary. For evals we recommend using greedy/beam to get consistent comparators.
[31:05] [33:00] Lina: Ok, let's recap and align on next steps. Our asks: Jordan provide 1k representative prompts and entity metrics, Priya confirm network constraints and egress rules, Becky confirm procurement timeline. Redwood to provide pilot SOW, billing example, security packet, and the benchmark runbook.
[33:25] Jordan: Sounds good. Quick queue — Marcus, can you put conservative-INT8 as the recommended default in the proposal?
[33:30] Marcus: Yup, will do.
[33:36] Becky: For timelines — procurement can sign pilot within 2 weeks if pricing matches budget.
[33:42] Avery: Great. Anything else?
[33:45] Priya: One last: can you provide a short note on KMS integration for Private?
[33:49] Lina: We'll include a KMS integration matrix.
[34:00] [36:10] Marcus: Alright I'll stop screen share. Thanks everyone — we'll package the artifacts.
[36:22] Sam: Appreciated, that demo clarified a lot.
[36:26] Jordan: Thank you.
[36:30] Avery: Thanks all — we'll follow up with SOW and scripts.
[36:36] Becky: Thanks.
[36:40] Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-heard product terminology and shorthand; some names were abbreviated in call. References: "pilot SOW" (link shared in chat), "benchmark script" (link to shared drive).
notes: Masking/PHI approach discussed — redaction for hosted demos, Private avoids token exposure
Conservative-INT8 recommended as compromise (latency gains, <3% quality delta)
